questions.domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML
questions.stem: A retail chain wants to implement its first Machine Learning project on Amazon SageMaker AI to predict monthly customer churn. The CTO asks the team to arrange the following four ML lifecycle stages in chronological order from project inception to production: 1. Feature engineering and data cleansing using SageMaker Data Wrangler. 2. Defining the business goal and framing the ML problem. 3. Model training, hyperparameter tuning, and metric evaluation. 4. Endpoint deployment and continuous monitoring with SageMaker Model Monitor. What is the correct sequence?
questions.explanation: Every ML lifecycle starts by defining the business goal and problem framing (2), followed by data preparation and feature engineering (1), then model training and evaluation (3), and finally deployment and continuous monitoring (4). Options A, C, and D place downstream technical tasks ahead of prerequisites.
questions.use_case: In enterprise MLOps, aligning the business KPI before touching data prevents building accurate models that solve the wrong business problem.
questions.hack: Golden MLOps sequence: Business Goal (2) -> Data/Features (1) -> Train/Eval (3) -> Deploy/Monitor (4).

questions.domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML
questions.stem: A solutions architect is designing four workloads on Amazon SageMaker AI with different latency and payload requirements. Match each numbered scenario to the appropriate inference mode: 1. Credit card payment authorization requiring sub-30-millisecond responses 24/7. 2. An internal HR tool that receives sporadic queries during business hours and sits idle nights and weekends. 3. Processing 750 MB medical video files that take 12 minutes per request using an internal queue. 4. Scoring purchase propensity for 15 million customer records stored in Amazon S3 every Sunday night. Which option shows the correct matching?
options: 1: Serverless Inference | 2: Real-Time Inference | 3: Batch Transform | 4: Asynchronous Inference
1: Real-Time Inference | 2: Asynchronous Inference | 3: Serverless Inference | 4: Batch Transform
1: Real-Time Inference | 2: Serverless Inference | 3: Asynchronous Inference | 4: Batch Transform
1: Batch Transform | 2: Serverless Inference | 3: Asynchronous Inference | 4: Real-Time Inference
questions.explanation: Real-Time Inference keeps endpoints warm 24/7 for millisecond latency (1). Serverless Inference scales down to zero during idle periods (2). Asynchronous Inference handles payloads up to 1 GB and processing times up to 1 hour with built-in queuing (3). Batch Transform scores massive offline S3 datasets without persistent endpoints (4).
questions.use_case: Matching traffic patterns to the right SageMaker AI inference mode prevents paying 24/7 GPU costs for nightly batch or intermittent internal workloads.
questions.hack: ms 24/7 = Real-Time; Scale to 0 = Serverless; Up to 1 GB / 1 hr queued = Async; Offline S3 millions = Batch Transform.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML
questions.stem: A data science team trains a deep neural network on Amazon SageMaker AI to classify insurance claims. The model achieves 98.7% accuracy on the training dataset but drops to 61.4% accuracy on the validation dataset. Which TWO technical actions should the team take to resolve this issue? (Choose TWO)
options: Apply regularization techniques such as Dropout or L1/L2 penalties and enable Early Stopping during training.
Increase the number of training epochs from 50 to 500 and add more hidden layers to the neural network.
Increase the size and diversity of the training dataset or apply Data Augmentation.
Remove the validation split so the model trains on 100% of available records.
Reduce the training dataset size and disable k-fold cross-validation.
questions.explanation: Very high training accuracy (98.7%) paired with low validation accuracy (61.4%) indicates Overfitting. Overfitting is mitigated by applying regularization (Dropout, L1/L2) and Early Stopping (A), as well as expanding training data diversity or using Data Augmentation (C). Adding more layers and epochs (B) worsens overfitting.
questions.use_case: Enabling Early Stopping in SageMaker AI training jobs both prevents overfitting and cuts unnecessary GPU billing hours.
questions.hack: 99% Train vs 61% Validation = Overfitting -> Regularization (Dropout/L1/L2) + Early Stopping + More diverse data.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML
questions.stem: A digital bank processes 2 million daily transfers where 99.85% are legitimate transactions and only 0.15% are actual fraud. A data scientist presents a classifier boasting 99.85% Accuracy, but the security team discovers the model caught zero fraudulent transfers all week. Which evaluation metric should the bank use to properly balance catching real fraud against avoiding false alarms on legitimate customers?
options: Mean Squared Error (MSE).
ROUGE-L.
R-squared (R²).
F1-Score (or Precision-Recall AUC).
questions.explanation: On heavily imbalanced datasets (99.85% vs. 0.15%), Accuracy is misleading because a model that always predicts 'legitimate' scores 99.85% while catching zero fraud. F1-Score (the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall) properly evaluates minority-class classification. MSE and R² are regression metrics, and ROUGE-L evaluates text summarization.
questions.use_case: In payment fraud pipelines, MLOps deployment gates validate F1-Score and Recall at specific precision thresholds rather than overall Accuracy.
questions.hack: Imbalanced dataset (fraud/rare events) -> Ignore Accuracy and select F1-Score.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML
questions.stem: A logistics company runs a regression model on Amazon SageMaker AI that predicts package delivery times using only 3 input variables. Because the model suffers from underfitting, the technical lead asks the team to increase the number of input variables by deriving new columns from timestamps, weather logs, and historical routes. Which process and AWS tool should the team use?
options: Feature Engineering using Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler.
Hyperparameter Tuning using Amazon SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning.
Model compilation using Amazon SageMaker Neo.
Dimensionality reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA).
questions.explanation: Creating new input variables from raw data to improve model learning is Feature Engineering, which is visually accelerated by Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler. Hyperparameter Tuning (B) adjusts training settings like learning rate or epochs—it never adds input features. PCA (D) reduces rather than increases feature count.
questions.use_case: Data scientists use SageMaker Data Wrangler to visually create time-window aggregations and interaction features before training.
questions.hack: 'Increase the number of input variables' = Feature Engineering (Data Wrangler), NEVER Hyperparameter Tuning!

questions.domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML
questions.stem: An insurance provider receives 40,000 scanned PDF medical claim forms daily containing checkboxes, hospital billing tables, and handwritten physician notes. The engineering team needs to extract this information into structured JSON with minimal development effort. Which AWS service meets this requirement?
options: Amazon Rekognition.
Amazon Textract.
Amazon Comprehend Medical.
Amazon Kendra.
questions.explanation: Amazon Textract is purpose-built for intelligent document processing, extracting printed text, handwriting, checkboxes, form key-value pairs, and structured tables from scanned PDFs and images. Amazon Rekognition (A) detects objects and faces in photos/videos, while Comprehend Medical (C) requires plain text that has already been extracted.
questions.use_case: Production claims pipelines run scanned PDFs through Amazon Textract (`AnalyzeDocument` with `TABLES` and `FORMS`) before passing extracted text downstream.
questions.hack: Scanned PDFs + tables + forms + handwriting = Amazon Textract.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML
questions.stem: An e-commerce platform has 8 million shopper profiles containing browsing behavior and purchase totals, but the dataset has no prior labels or categories. The marketing team wants to discover natural customer groups with similar buying habits to design targeted campaigns. Which learning paradigm and algorithm are most appropriate?
options: Supervised Learning using the k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN) algorithm.
Reinforcement Learning using a reward-maximization policy.
Unsupervised Learning using the k-Means clustering algorithm.
Supervised Learning using multiclass logistic regression.
questions.explanation: When data is unlabeled and the goal is to group records by similarity into natural segments, the task is Clustering under Unsupervised Learning using algorithms such as k-Means. Both k-NN (A) and logistic regression (D) are supervised algorithms that require pre-existing target labels.
questions.use_case: Marketing analytics teams run SageMaker AI's built-in k-Means algorithm on unlabeled transaction logs to discover distinct buyer personas.
questions.hack: Unlabeled data + group similar customers = Unsupervised Clustering with k-Means (do not confuse with supervised k-NN!).

questions.domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML
questions.stem: A hospital needs to build two workflows: first, medical specialists must label 25,000 chest X-rays stored in Amazon S3 before training a model; second, once deployed in production, any prediction with a confidence score below 85% must automatically route to a human radiologist for review. Which combination of AWS services should the hospital select?
options: Amazon A2I for pre-training dataset labeling and Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth for production prediction review.
Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels for both tasks without human workflows.
Amazon SageMaker Clarify for initial labeling and Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor for human review.
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth for pre-training dataset labeling and Amazon Augmented AI (Amazon A2I) for low-confidence production review.
questions.explanation: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth manages human labeling workflows (and active learning) to build training datasets BEFORE model training. Amazon Augmented AI (Amazon A2I) provides human-in-the-loop review of low-confidence predictions IN PRODUCTION.
questions.use_case: Using Ground Truth pre-training and A2I in live inference creates a flywheel where human-verified edge cases feed back into future training sets.
questions.hack: Humans BEFORE training = Ground Truth; Humans IN PRODUCTION for low confidence = Amazon A2I.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML
questions.stem: A team of financial analysts with no coding or data science background wants to build quarterly sales forecasts from historical data in Amazon Redshift and Amazon S3 using a visual point-and-click interface. Meanwhile, the ML engineering team wants to run an AutoML experiment that produces inspectable Python notebooks showing every step of the code. Which tool should each team use?
options: The financial analysts should use Amazon SageMaker Canvas, and the ML engineers should use Amazon SageMaker Autopilot.
The financial analysts should use Amazon SageMaker Autopilot, and the ML engineers should use Amazon SageMaker Canvas.
Both teams should use Amazon SageMaker Neo.
The analysts should use Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth, and the engineers should use Amazon SageMaker Clarify.
questions.explanation: Amazon SageMaker Canvas provides a visual, no-code interface tailored for business and financial analysts. Amazon SageMaker Autopilot is a white-box AutoML capability that automatically explores algorithms and generates full Jupyter notebooks with Python code for engineers to inspect and customize.
questions.use_case: Giving business analysts SageMaker Canvas for tabular forecasting frees ML engineers to focus on production pipelines with Autopilot.
questions.hack: No-code business analyst = SageMaker Canvas; AutoML with inspectable Python code = SageMaker Autopilot.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML
questions.stem: During a technical review of a neural network training job in Amazon SageMaker AI, a junior developer confuses which elements the model learns automatically during backpropagation and which elements the engineer must configure before launching the training job. Which statement correctly distinguishes model parameters from hyperparameters?
options: Learning rate and epochs are internal parameters learned by the network, whereas synaptic weights are hyperparameters set manually.
Weights and biases are model parameters learned automatically during training, whereas learning rate, batch size, and number of epochs are hyperparameters configured before training.
Both weights and learning rate are hyperparameters that remain constant throughout training.
Hyperparameters are the input CSV columns, and parameters are evaluation metrics like ROUGE and BLEU.
questions.explanation: Model parameters (weights and biases) are internal values updated automatically by the optimization algorithm during training. Hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, epochs, network depth) are external configuration settings specified before the training job begins.
questions.use_case: When configuring SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning, you specify search ranges for hyperparameters like `learning_rate` so each trial learns optimal model weights.
questions.hack: Weights & biases = learned internally by the model; Hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, epochs) = set externally before training.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML
questions.stem: A telemedicine clinic records audio consultations and uses Amazon Transcribe to generate clinical notes automatically. However, physicians notice that brand-new medication names and hospital-specific acronyms are frequently misspelled in the transcripts. What is the most direct way to improve transcription accuracy for these specific terms?
options: Replace Amazon Transcribe with Amazon Polly using SSML tags.
Use Amazon Comprehend to translate the audio stream before transcription.
Configure a Custom Vocabulary in Amazon Transcribe containing the list of medication names and acronyms.
Train a diffusion model from scratch in Amazon SageMaker AI.
questions.explanation: Amazon Transcribe Custom Vocabulary lets you supply a list of domain-specific words, brand names, drug names, and acronyms (with optional phonetic hints) so the speech-to-text engine recognizes them accurately. Amazon Polly (A) converts text to speech rather than speech to text.
questions.use_case: Uploading a table of company product names and acronyms to an Amazon Transcribe Custom Vocabulary immediately fixes proper-noun recognition errors.
questions.hack: Specific brand names, drug names, or acronyms in speech-to-text = Amazon Transcribe Custom Vocabulary.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML
questions.stem: An energy corporation has four data science teams that independently compute the same household electricity consumption variables for different models on Amazon SageMaker AI. In production, models underperform because the SQL logic used during batch training differs slightly from the logic used during real-time API inference (training-serving skew). Which AWS service eliminates duplicate engineering work and guarantees feature consistency between training and inference?
options: Amazon SageMaker Model Registry.
Amazon SageMaker Clarify.
Amazon Augmented AI (Amazon A2I).
Amazon SageMaker Feature Store.
questions.explanation: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store provides a centralized repository to store, share, and reuse ML features across teams. By offering both an Offline Store (for batch training) and a low-latency Online Store (for real-time inference) backed by the exact same feature definitions, it eliminates training-serving skew.
questions.use_case: Centralizing engineered features in SageMaker Feature Store ensures every model trains and serves predictions using identical feature values.
questions.hack: Share features across teams + prevent training-serving skew = Amazon SageMaker Feature Store.

questions.domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML
questions.stem: A wind turbine manufacturer trained a PyTorch computer vision model in Amazon SageMaker AI to detect blade micro-fractures. Now the company must deploy this model directly onto smart cameras powered by ARM processors at remote wind farms with limited internet connectivity, requiring a smaller memory footprint and twice the inference speed. Which capability should they use?
options: Amazon SageMaker Neo.
Amazon SageMaker Batch Transform.
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth.
questions.explanation: Amazon SageMaker Neo compiles ML models trained in PyTorch, TensorFlow, or XGBoost into optimized binaries tailored for specific target hardware (ARM, Intel, NVIDIA edge devices or cloud instances), running up to 2x faster with a minimal memory footprint.
questions.use_case: Compile vision models with SageMaker Neo before deploying them to industrial edge cameras managed by AWS IoT Greengrass.
questions.hack: Compile and optimize ML models for edge hardware = Amazon SageMaker Neo.

questions.stem: An AI engineer is explaining how a Transformer-based language model processes an input sentence to generate the first output token. Arrange the following 4 internal stages in chronological order: 1. The Softmax layer converts output logits into a probability distribution to sample the next token. 2. The tokenizer splits raw text into subword tokens and maps them to numerical token IDs. 3. Self-Attention layers weigh the contextual relevance of every token against all other tokens in parallel. 4. The Embedding layer maps each token ID to a dense vector and adds Positional Encoding to preserve word order. What is the correct sequence?
questions.explanation: First, raw text is tokenized into token IDs (2); second, token IDs are converted into dense embeddings plus Positional Encoding (4); third, Self-Attention layers compute contextual relationships in parallel (3); finally, the Softmax layer converts raw logits into token probabilities (1).
questions.use_case: Understanding this pipeline explains why long prompts increase both input token charges (step 2) and attention memory overhead (step 3).
questions.hack: Transformer flow: Tokenize (2) -> Embedding + Positional Encoding (4) -> Self-Attention (3) -> Softmax (1).

questions.stem: An advertising studio uses image diffusion models in Amazon Bedrock (such as Amazon Nova Canvas) and needs to match four technical concepts to their exact functions: 1. Replacing only a model's shirt inside an existing photograph using a mask. 2. Expanding a 1:1 square photo outward on the sides to turn it into a seamless 16:9 panoramic banner. 3. The process of iteratively removing Gaussian noise step by step to construct a sharp image guided by text. 4. The parameter controlling how strictly the generated image adheres to the text prompt versus creative freedom. Which option shows the correct matching?
options: 1: Outpainting | 2: Inpainting | 3: Forward Diffusion | 4: Temperature
1: Inpainting | 2: Outpainting | 3: Positional Encoding | 4: Top-K
1: Inpainting | 2: Outpainting | 3: Reverse Diffusion | 4: Guidance Scale (Prompt Strength)
1: Reverse Diffusion | 2: Guidance Scale | 3: Inpainting | 4: Outpainting
questions.explanation: Inpainting edits a masked region inside an image (1); Outpainting extends the canvas outside original borders (2); Reverse Diffusion iteratively denoises an image (3); and Guidance Scale (Prompt Strength) controls how tightly the image follows the prompt (4).
questions.use_case: Creative teams use Amazon Nova Canvas Inpainting to swap product props and Outpainting to resize assets across ad formats.
questions.hack: INpainting = inside mask; OUTpainting = outside borders; Reverse Diffusion = denoise; Guidance Scale = prompt adherence.
